findings: Premise and edit target unverifiable: no src tree in the repo, and the prerequisite and related tickets don't exist: The plan rests on a CLOSED prerequisite epic 8f6c-6008-33f3-4f82 with code under `src/rebar/grounding/`, and says it will 'depends_on' it. The plan also cites the follow-on ticket `850f` and the consumer `9da1`. None of these tickets can be found in the ticket store, so neither the 'CLOSED' claim nor the dependency link can be checked. The repo under review has no `src/` at all, just a README and `.rebar/hlc.state`. The facade symbols resolve only from an installed copy in a different worktree (phoebe-harness). The plan also never names which files or modules it will create or change: where P1–P8 live, where tests go, or where the attestation's coverage field is defined.

P8 is missing from the fail-open/test criterion and the title (P1–P7 vs P1–P8 drift): The title and the first acceptance criterion cover only P1–P7: 'implemented ... polyglot, fail-open (skipped=pass) tested per tool'. P8 was added later and appears only in its own criterion and the T8 criterion ('P1–P8'). So nothing requires P8 to be fail-open or tested on its abstain path, and the scope numbering contradicts itself.

P8 inputs and ownership are not defined: P8 FAILs, inside the only blocking tier, when content 'is anticipated (token-estimate) to exceed the largest configured context window'. The plan never says which tokenizer or estimator is used, where 'largest configured context window' comes from, or what a 'parent+child pairing for container criteria' is. It also says both that P8 lives in the DET floor and that 'the orchestrator emits it during the size-handling ladder', which leaves two possible owners. An implementer can't build this, or set a blocking threshold, without asking.

Undefined check meanings (P5 'interference', P6 'AC/DD quality', P7 'escalates T4'): Several checks are named but never defined. P5 'interference', P6 'AC/DD quality' ('DD' is never expanded) and P7 'escalates T4' have no stated rules. Nothing says what a deterministic AC-quality check looks at, what counts as interference between DAG tasks, or whether P7's escalation blocks, warns, or sends the plan to an LLM tier. Since this is the blocking floor, vague rules mean unpredictable false blocks.

Fail-open with 'skipped = PASS' in the only blocking tier lets coverage silently collapse: The DET floor is the only tier that blocks. When ctags, scc/lizard or network access is missing (for example on a bare CI image), P2–P4 abstain and count as PASS. The floor then lets everything through and nothing has to react. 'Coverage recorded on the attestation' has no defined format, and no consumer is required to warn when coverage is degraded or zero. As written, the 'ironclad' guarantee also guarantees silent degradation.

Testing covers only fail-open paths, not detection correctness: The only test requirement is 'fail-open (skipped=pass) tested per tool'. Nothing requires tests showing that P1/P5/P6/P7 actually flag bad input (missing readiness fields, cyclic DAG, destructive verbs) and pass good input. Nothing lists which tools or languages make up 'polyglot', so 'per tool' can't be checked either.

'Why' contradicts the blocking criterion: 'Why' says the DET floor is the ONLY blocking tier and every LLM criterion is advisory in v1. The third criterion says LLM-tier blocking can be opted into per criterion via `block_threshold`, so DET-only is just a default. The sections disagree on whether LLM tiers can block in v1. That criterion also describes the whole system's posture and orchestrator config, not something this child delivers, so it can't be verified from this child's work.

deps.dev registry lookups conflict with a 'frozen, deterministic' floor: P3 asks a live network registry (deps.dev) whether packages exist. Its results change over time (packages get published or yanked) and depend on network access, so the same plan can pass one day and block the next. That breaks the stated goal of a 'frozen, deterministic' floor, and the plan doesn't address it: no pinning, snapshot or cache policy.

Fail-open is specified only for oracle-backed checks (P2/P3/P4). The plan does not define what happens when a rebar-owned check (P1/P5/P6/P7/P8) raises or gets malformed input, such as an unparseable task DAG or a missing context-window config. If the check crashes, the floor errors and blocks everything. If it is swallowed as PASS, P7's destructive/irreversible escalation is silently lost.

P7 is listed as part of the DET floor, which is the only blocking tier in v1, but it is described only as 'escalates T4'. The plan never says whether a P7 hit blocks, only escalates to an LLM criterion that is advisory by default, or both. If it only escalates, the destructive/irreversible check, which is the one most worth blocking on, never blocks by default.

The rebar-specific checks this child owns (P1 readiness-shape, P5 task-DAG validity + interference, P6 AC/DD quality, P7 destructive/irreversible sniff) are only named, never specified. No deterministic rule, input field, or pass/fail condition is given, so the executor must invent the core logic of the blocking tier.

Two numeric limits are unstated, and so is their source. P4 oversize has no threshold (scc/lizard metric and limit). P8 does not say where the 'largest configured context window' is configured or how the token estimate is computed.

The only testing AC covers the skip path ('fail-open (skipped=pass) tested per tool'). No AC requires each check to actually FAIL on a known-bad fixture, e.g. an unresolvable symbol for P2, a nonexistent package for P3, an oversize file for P4, a cyclic or interfering DAG for P5, a destructive op escalating T4 for P7, an over-budget ticket for P8. The block path of the only blocking tier is untested.

Most acceptance criteria are effort-framed and have no proving command. 'P1-P7 implemented in Python' describes effort, not an observable outcome. 'fail-open tested per tool' lists no abstain-reason fixtures. The posture AC ('only tier that blocks BY DEFAULT') and the exec=DET dispatch AC have no check that would produce evidence.

'Coverage recorded on the attestation' is an output field with no stated schema or provenance. It is unclear what 'coverage' measures (checks run vs. abstained? languages covered? per-check abstain reasons?) and which attestation field holds it. The plan body never describes this deliverable, so the AC is an orphan.

The ticket bundles eight heterogeneous checks with different tools and failure modes (P1–P8), the P2/P3/P4 oracle wiring, and a new first-class exec=DET execution path, accreted via two '(Added)' sections. There is no stated sequencing or thin slice: for example, exec=DET dispatch plus one check end-to-end first, then the rest. It is unclear this executes as one session. 'DET floor' is a coherent concern, so this is a sequencing/size observation rather than a demand to split.

The plan calls the floor 'frozen, deterministic', yet P3 uses live deps.dev registry lookups. Results can change over time, and the lookup carries network, rate-limit and auth constraints. A ticket could pass today and block tomorrow with no ticket change. The plan does not acknowledge this.

The floor is declared 'frozen, deterministic', but P3 queries the live deps.dev registry, and P2/P4 depend on external tool versions (ctags/scc/lizard/syft). The same ticket can therefore get different P3/P4 verdicts over time or across machines. The plan never says how determinism is preserved (pinned tool versions, a registry snapshot/cache, or recording the registry response on the attestation).

P8 has two different execution placements. Its own section says the orchestrator emits it 'during the size-handling ladder'. The T8 AC says P1–P8 are dispatched uniformly as the exec=DET tier via the code executor. The plan also leaves 'parent+child pairing for container criteria' and the token-estimate method undefined, so the P8 pass/fail boundary is not reproducible.

P3 depends on the deps.dev registry, which is a live HTTPS network service, but the plan states no network or egress precondition. It also doesn't say how offline or unreachable-registry conditions map to the abstain contract, which only lists 'unsupported lang / no tool / parse-error / timeout'. Querying a live registry also clashes with the 'frozen, deterministic' floor claim, because the same input can give different results over time.

The title says the work builds 'fail-open polyglot tool wrappers', but Scope says the tooling is consumed from 8f6c 'as a library, not as new integrations'. The two sections conflict on whether this child writes wrappers.

The title promises building 'fail-open polyglot tool wrappers', but What/Scope state this child does NOT build them and only consumes the 8f6c facade. The first AC ('P1-P7 implemented in Python, polyglot … tested per tool') likewise demands implementing P2/P3/P4, which the scope says are consumed.

Atomic submit needs per-change Verified votes, which the plan scopes out: In Gerrit, submitting the tip of a relation chain only lands it together with its ancestors if every change in the chain meets the submit requirements, normally including Verified+1. The plan says verified-casting is a separate story, so Verified isn't cast on each batched change and AC3 (atomic submit on green) can't be met within this story. Also, rebasing each change to build the combined chain creates new patch sets, which can drop non-sticky Code-Review/Verified votes. The plan doesn't address this.

No edit set, and the repo has no queue/Gerrit/CI code for the plan to extend: The plan doesn't name a single file, module or service to change. The repository it will touch has no Autosubmit queue, no Gerrit client, no CI-trigger code and no workflow files. All it holds is a one-line README and a rebar clock file. An implementer can't tell where the batching assembler, the single-run trigger or the atomic-land step should go, or what Phase 1 code they build on.

The Phase 1 dependency can't be traced to anything: 'Depends on Phase 1' gives no ticket id or artifact. No S-series tickets can be found, so nobody can check what Phase 1 supplies (the queue, the Autosubmit label handling, the CI bridge) or whether it exists.

'Tested tip == landed tree' isn't guaranteed if main moves: The plan builds the chain on the current main tip and tests it once, but doesn't say what happens if main moves between triggering CI and submitting. Depending on the project's submit strategy, Gerrit may rebase or merge the chain onto the new main, and the landed tree would then differ from the one that was tested. That breaks the plan's central correctness promise. No fast-forward-only, re-test, or abort-on-moved-base rule is given.

No mechanism for triggering GHA on a Gerrit chain, and per-change triggers could break 'exactly ONE run': GitHub Actions doesn't trigger on Gerrit changes natively. The plan doesn't say how the combined tip reaches GHA: a push to a mirror or batch ref, workflow_dispatch, or repository_dispatch. It also doesn't say how the per-patchset CI triggers that fire when each change is rebased into the chain are suppressed, so AC2 ('exactly ONE CI run') could be violated by the assembly step itself.

The batch-size bound mixes up concurrent runs and jobs per run, and its premise is unverified: AC4 bounds batch size by 'one CI run's job budget (fits the GHA concurrency cap)', but the cap the plan cites is '~3 concurrent runs'. A single run takes one run slot whatever the batch size. GHA concurrency limits apply to concurrent jobs, not to the number of changes in one run, so batch size doesn't map onto the cap. The '~3 concurrent runs' Free-tier figure is asserted with no source. As written, the bound can't be computed or checked.

Rebase conflicts while assembling the chain aren't handled: Building one linear chain from independent stacks means rebasing each stack onto the previous one, and this can conflict. Batch-failure handling is scoped out, but an assembly conflict happens before CI and isn't a batch CI failure. The plan doesn't say whether a conflicting stack is skipped, ejected from the batch, or aborts the whole batch.

No testing plan: The plan has no tests: nothing for chain assembly order, for a single run starting, for atomic submit landing the exact tested tree, or for the batch-size bound. Without them, AC2 and AC3 have no evidence beyond assertion.

No rollout or kill-switch back to serial landing: Batching changes how every queued change lands, but the plan has no flag to turn it on or off and no fallback to serial per-change landing if batching misbehaves.

AC3 assumes that submitting the combined tip is 'ancestor-atomic' and that 'the tested tip == the landed tree'. Whether that holds depends on Gerrit's submit type and project config, and on `main` not moving between the CI run and the submit. The repo has no Gerrit config, and the plan says nothing about either condition. With rebase-always or cherry-pick submit types, or merge-if-necessary after `main` advances, the landed tree is not the tested tip.

'The tested tip == the landed tree' is asserted, but nothing enforces it. This is a check-then-act race. main can advance between assembly/CI start and submit, and any change in the batch can get a new patchset while CI runs. Depending on the submit strategy, Gerrit may then rebase or merge at submit time, so the landed tree is one CI never tested. The plan gives no guard: no fast-forward-only check, no compare of the base/patchset SHAs at submit time, no abort-and-rebatch.

'Tested tip == landed tree' only holds under certain conditions. The project's submit type must not rewrite commits (e.g. Fast Forward Only, or Merge If Necessary when the chain sits exactly on the tip), and main must not move between the CI run and the submit. The plan states neither condition and gives no re-check or abort step for when main moves.

The plan does not say what happens if `main` advances while the batch's CI run is in flight. Rebasing the batch before submit would land a tree that was never tested, which contradicts AC3's 'tested tip == the landed tree'. The plan names no fast-forward-only rule and no rebase/retest policy.

There is no guard against `main` advancing between assembling the batch / triggering CI and submitting it. This is a check-then-act TOCTOU. If Gerrit rebases on submit or merges onto a newer main, the landed tree differs from the tested tip, which violates AC3.

The plan does not define how batch membership is frozen during the CI run. Mid-run, an author may upload a new patchset, remove Autosubmit, lose a vote, or abandon a change in the batch, and the plan does not say how that invalidates the tested tip.

The batch-size bound is tied to the wrong variable. One CI run on the combined tip runs the same jobs however many changes the batch holds, so the batch size doesn't affect the GHA job budget or the concurrency cap. What batch size actually changes is the chance that a batch fails and the cost of isolating the bad change.

The plan does not account for the side effects of uploading rebased patchsets for every change in the combined chain. (a) Depending on label copy conditions, Code-Review or other votes may be dropped, so the atomic submit fails. (b) Each new patchset may trigger the existing per-change (Phase 1) CI, which contradicts 'exactly ONE CI run' and floods the ~3-run concurrency cap.

AC4 says the batch size is 'bounded to one CI run's job budget' but never gives the bound or its unit (changes? stacks? GHA jobs?). It also conflates a per-run job budget with the '~3 concurrent runs' cap, which concerns concurrent runs, not jobs within one run. 'documents the bound' does not say where.

The batch-size bound is ill-defined. 'One CI run's job budget' and 'the GHA concurrency cap (~3 concurrent runs)' are different limits. A single run on the combined tip has a job count that does not obviously scale with batch size, so it is unclear what actually caps N. There is also no concrete number and no wall-clock done-definition for a batch cycle.

Assembly-time failure is unhandled. When stacking one queued stack onto another yields a merge conflict, the plan does not say whether the conflicting stack is excluded, the batch is aborted, or the author is notified. This is distinct from CI-red batch failure, which is the deferred story.

The assembly algorithm is undefined. The plan does not say how queued `Autosubmit` changes are discovered (label, hashtag, Phase 1 queue API?), what order stacks are concatenated in, or what happens when a stack fails to rebase cleanly onto the previous one. The plan defers batch-*failure* handling, but assembly-time conflicts are part of assembly itself.

AC3 requires submitting the whole batch 'on green', but Scope says 'Verified-casting ... [is a] separate stor[y]'. The plan never says how each change in the combined chain obtains the Verified (and Code-Review) votes that Gerrit submit requirements need. Without those votes the ancestor submit cannot proceed.

The 'Free-tier GHA concurrency cap (~3 concurrent runs)' premise has no source. It also mixes up workflow 'runs' and 'jobs', which are different things. GitHub's concurrency limits are documented per job and per runner OS. The plan uses this number both to justify batching (Why) and to set the batch-size bound (AC4), so the bound has no verified basis.

Ancestor-atomic submit in Gerrit only succeeds if every change in the chain meets its submit requirements (e.g. Verified+1, Code-Review+2). Verified-casting is declared a separate story, and the plan depends only on Phase 1. So the 'on green, submit' step has an unstated dependency on Verified being cast on every change from the single combined run.

The assembly step doesn't cover the case where queued stacks conflict with each other, or with main, when combined. It also doesn't say how the queue is snapshotted while new Autosubmit changes keep arriving during a run.

AC2 ('exactly ONE CI run') can conflict with the assembly mechanism. Rebasing each queued change into the chain uploads a new patchset per change. If CI triggers on patchset-created/push (the usual Gerrit→GHA setup), that starts N runs, which uses up the ~3-run concurrency cap that batching is meant to protect.

The plan's main reason for batching over speculation, and its AC4 batch-size bound, rest on an unchecked platform limit: 'Free-tier GHA concurrency cap (~3 concurrent runs)'. The sources I retrieved say GitHub Free allows 20 concurrent jobs on standard GitHub-hosted runners (5 for macOS). That number would change the speculation-vs-batching tradeoff and the size of the 'one CI run's job budget' bound.

The plan assumes Gerrit gives 'ancestor-atomic submit' with 'the tested tip == the landed tree' but never checks this against Gerrit's submit strategies or the multi-repo case. Gerrit lets each project pick a submit strategy. With rebase or cherry-pick strategies, and if main moves between CI and submit, the landed commits differ from the tested tip. A single relation chain also can't span projects, so 'cross-stack' batches across repos would need topic-based submitWholeTopic semantics instead.

Rebasing queued changes onto each other to form the combined chain creates new patch sets. Whether Code-Review/Autosubmit votes carry over depends on the labels' copyCondition settings, and conflicting rebases drop them. Ancestor submit also needs every change in the chain to meet its submit requirements, including Verified, but the plan pushes Verified-casting to a separate story. So AC3 can't be met by this story alone.

The batch-size bound rests on an unverified figure: '~3 concurrent runs' for the GHA Free tier. GitHub's published Free-plan limits are stated as concurrent jobs, not runs, and my recollection is that the Free-plan figure is higher than 3 (unconfirmed, from memory). The plan doesn't cite a source or say how the 'job budget' maps to a batch size.

Plan relies on code, a workflow and tickets that aren't in the repo: The plan says it reuses S2's selection, rebase and `is:submittable` machinery, uses `/rebase:chain` as the building block, and dispatches `gerrit-verify.yaml`. Its rationale also depends on that workflow's per-change concurrency group. None of these can be found in the repository, and the S2 dependency ticket cannot be found under either its alias or its id. The plan also names no files or modules to create or change. An implementer cannot tell where batching goes, what interface it calls, or whether the premise about the concurrency group (the basis of the 'Why') is true.

Handoff record has no base `main` SHA, so the stale-tree check can't be repeated at submit time: S7 checks for staleness 'immediately before the batch is handed off', but S8 does the vote-casting and the submit later. `main` can advance in that window, so the TOCTOU is not closed. The record `{member_change_ids[], combined_tip_change_id, tested_sha, run_id}` holds the tested tip SHA but not the `main` SHA the chain was built on. S8 therefore cannot check that the tested tree is still based on the current `main`, which defeats the AC's own 'never hand off a stale tree' goal.

Cross-stack assembly rewrites users' real changes and never restores them: Building a combined chain from separate stacks with `/rebase:chain` uploads new patchsets that re-parent stack B onto stack A's tip in Gerrit. The plan never says what happens to this new parentage when the batch is dropped to the serial path after N=5 attempts, or when it fails (S9). If nothing restores it, unrelated stacks stay coupled: A's failure blocks B, and the serial lander sees one large merged chain instead of separate stacks. The plan doesn't address rollback, reversibility or ownership of this shared Gerrit state.

No rule for a member that conflicts during assembly: The 'Why' depends on combining non-conflicting changes, but the plan never says how conflicts are found or handled during assembly, e.g. when the rebase returns a conflict (409) for one member. Batch-failure handling is assigned to S9, but that covers CI failure after the run, not conflicts while S7 is building the chain. The implementer has to guess whether to exclude the member, abort the batch, or fall back to serial.

'Exactly ONE CI run' conflicts with the re-batch loop, and the ~1-cycle claim ignores re-batches: AC2 requires exactly one CI run, but AC3 re-assembles and re-batches up to 5 times. Each re-assembly produces a new tree that needs a fresh CI run, so a batch can trigger up to 6 runs. That breaks AC2 as written and weakens the 'collapses it to ~1 CI cycle' rationale whenever `main` moves often. The plan also doesn't say whether a re-batch cancels the in-flight run or what happens to the old `run_id`.

Location, lifetime and concurrency rules of the batch state are undefined: The handoff record goes to 'the batch state', which the plan never defines: where it is stored, who clears it, what happens to stale records after a drop or re-batch, and how the batch lander and the Phase-1 serial lander avoid claiming the same changes. The plan admits the single-`wipChain` invariant no longer holds but names only the re-batch loop as the mitigation. That loop deals with `main` advancing, not with two landers racing over the same members.

Plan has no testing section: The plan has no tests or verification steps for assembly order, enforcing the BATCH_MAX=8 cap, dispatching exactly one run against the real tip patchset, the N=5 re-batch bound and fallback, or the shape of the handoff record. Several ACs, such as 'never loop unbounded', can only be shown with an automated test against a fake Gerrit or GHA.

Stated reason for BATCH_MAX=8 doesn't hold: The cap is justified as 'sized to one run's job budget under the GHA concurrency cap'. But the combined tip is tested by a single run of `gerrit-verify.yaml`, whose job count doesn't depend on how many members are in the chain, so member count doesn't consume job budget. The real costs of a larger batch are the blast radius and bisection cost when a run fails (S9), and longer assembly. Without a sound reason, nobody can later tell whether 8 is right.

Conflict handling during assembly is undefined. The What says the algorithm combines 'N non-conflicting changes', but no AC says what happens when stacking stack B onto stack A conflicts. The member could be excluded and left for the next batch, the whole batch could abort, or the conflict could fall back to the serial path.

The plan has no handling for a rebase conflict during cross-stack assembly. The What says batching combines 'N non-conflicting changes', but no AC says how conflicts are detected or what happens when /rebase:chain fails partway. Options include excluding the offending stack and retrying, or aborting and leaving the members untouched.

The plan never says what happens when one stack doesn't apply cleanly on top of the others during assembly. The Why/What text assumes 'N non-conflicting changes', but no AC says how conflicts are found, which stack is left out, or how the remaining stacks are ordered.
The mechanism for 'dropped to the Phase-1 serial path' is undefined. The plan does not say how members are returned to the serial queue or whether their re-parented patchsets are restored first.

The batch-state handoff record has an incomplete lifecycle.
- Where it lives (Gerrit hashtag or comment, lander DB, file) is unspecified.
- Who may write it concurrently is undefined.
- It has no retire or supersede path. After a re-batch, the old `{tested_sha, run_id}` record must be invalidated so S8 cannot cast Verified against a stale SHA. After S8 lands, or after a fallback to serial, the record must be cleaned up.

Concurrency ownership between the batch lander and the Phase-1 serial lander (and between multiple batch runs) is undefined. Nothing prevents a change from being selected by both paths at once, or from appearing in two batches.

Assembling independent stacks into one linear chain permanently changes existing behavior: later stacks' changes are rebased onto other authors' changes, creating new cross-stack parent dependencies in Gerrit. The plan does not acknowledge this. It also does not say what happens to those dependencies when a batch is dropped to serial or fails. If they are not restored, a dropped stack B stays chained behind A and cannot land independently.

Assembly gives the real changes new cross-stack parents: stack B's base is rebased onto stack A's tip. The plan doesn't say what happens to that rewritten topology when the batch is dropped to the Phase-1 serial path after N=5 re-batches, or when CI fails (handed to S9). The serial path would then get changes that now depend on unrelated stacks, so 'serial' landing of B would quietly drag A in with it, or be blocked by it.

The location and format of the 'batch state' holding the handoff record are unspecified. Options include a Gerrit hashtag, a change message, a file in the repo, a CI artifact, or a DB. S8 must read it and S7 must write it, yet neither the store nor any versioning of the schema is defined.

Assembly rebases independent stacks onto each other, uploading new patchsets that make unrelated author changes dependent. This is a durable mutation of users' changes, and the plan has no back-out path, such as rebasing members back onto main, when a batch is abandoned or dropped. It also does not explicitly defer that path to S9.

The CI dispatch to gerrit-verify.yaml has no error handling. Nothing covers a dispatch API failure, a run that is queued indefinitely under the concurrency cap, or a run that never reports. There is no timeout, retry/backoff, or fallback for these cases.
It is unclear whether BATCH_MAX counts individual changes or whole stacks. If it counts changes, the plan does not say what happens to a single stack with more than 8 changes.

The rationale for BATCH_MAX=8 contradicts the Why section. The Why says the concurrent-run count isn't the limiter, because there is one combined-tip run per batch. Yet the cap is justified as 'sized to one run's job budget under the GHA concurrency cap'. A single run on the combined tip does not scale its job count with member count, so the stated sizing basis is unclear.

The reason given for BATCH_MAX=8, 'sized to one run's job budget under the GHA concurrency cap', contradicts the Why section. The Why says the concurrent-run count is not the limiter. It also doesn't explain how the number of members affects the job budget of one CI run on the combined tip. The constant looks like a cap borrowed from elsewhere without a stated reason.

The plan does not say how S7 obtains the run_id of the dispatched run or detects 'green'. A GHA workflow_dispatch call does not reliably return the created run's id, so a correlation method is needed (for example, a unique input echoed in the run name). No polling, webhook, or Gerrit-check mechanism is named for detecting completion.
Member ordering and selection are unspecified. When more than BATCH_MAX changes are queued, the plan does not say which members are picked, nor in what order stacks are placed in the combined chain.

Two edge cases at the cap and the re-batch boundary are undefined.
- A single stack with more than BATCH_MAX=8 members can never fit a batch. Splitting it mid-chain would break ancestor-atomicity, and the plan does not say what happens.
- How partially-fitting stacks are handled when filling to 8 (whole stacks only?) is also unspecified.
- Separately, each re-batch implies another full CI cycle, so a dropped batch can cost up to 6 CI cycles before serial even starts.

The TOCTOU re-check is a check-then-act that leaves a window. It only checks main advancement, and only 'before the batch is handed off', whereas S8 then casts votes and submits later. It also ignores membership drift during the batch: an author uploads a new patchset, removes Autosubmit, abandons a change, or a reviewer revokes a vote.

The TOCTOU re-check only looks at the `main` tip. The members can also change during the CI run: an author uploads a new patchset, Autosubmit is removed, or Code-Review drops. Any of these makes the tested tree or the eligibility stale while the check still passes. Also, a check run before handoff is check-then-act: `main` can still move between the check and S8's submit. What actually guarantees safety there is Gerrit rejecting a fast-forward-only submit, and the plan doesn't name that as the backstop.

The reason given for BATCH_MAX=8 doesn't fit the mechanism. A single CI run on the combined tip tests one tree, so its job count doesn't grow with the number of members, and 'sized to one run's job budget' doesn't explain the cap. The real constraints on batch size are the chance of failure or conflict per batch and how much a failure costs (bisection in S9), and those aren't mentioned.

The reason given for BATCH_MAX=8 ('sized to one run's job budget under the GHA concurrency cap') rests on a capability that doesn't fit. GitHub's Free-tier limit counts concurrent jobs per account (20). The plan sends exactly ONE gerrit-verify.yaml run against the combined tip, and that run's job count is set by the workflow, not by how many members are in the batch. So member count doesn't use up 'job budget', and the number 8 has no stated basis. In established batching designs (bors-style batches, merge-queue group-size caps), the batch-size cap is set by failure probability and the cost of bisecting a failed batch, not by runner concurrency.

AC2 requires S7 to record the dispatched run's `run_id` for S8. From general knowledge, the GitHub REST `workflow_dispatch` endpoint (`POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{workflow_id}/dispatches`) traditionally returns 204 with no body, so the dispatch response does not give a run_id. I could not check the current API docs here. The plan does not say how the run is linked to the dispatch, e.g. a unique correlation input reflected in `run-name` and then polling `GET .../actions/workflows/{id}/runs`. It also does not say whether it relies on a newer API option that returns run details.

The plan assumes Gerrit's `/rebase:chain` can be the building block for cross-stack chain assembly. As I understand Gerrit's REST API (outside knowledge, not checked with the tools), `rebase:chain` rebases one change's existing ancestor chain onto a base. It does not join separate, independent stacks into one linear chain. Joining stacks would mean re-parenting each stack's bottom change onto the previous stack's tip. The plan does not verify or describe that capability.

Coverage guard mostly re-checks slicing arithmetic and misses cross-worker divergence: The new guard checks that the concatenated chunks equal `_renderable_units()`. Both sides come from the same import-time list in the same process, so the check is close to a tautology: it confirms list slicing, not that each xdist worker parametrized the test over the same chunk contents. Each xdist worker imports the module and computes `_renderable_units()` on its own. xdist only compares node IDs (`[0]`..`[22]`), so if the unit order is not deterministic (for example unsorted directory listing or set iteration), workers can build different chunks under the same IDs. Units could then be silently skipped or compared twice, and the guard, running in a single worker, would still pass. The plan never requires `_renderable_units()` to return a stable, sorted order.
